ks1.objective: Play a fun tag game with a World Cup theme. Move safely, accept being tagged, and help teammates back into the game.
successCriteria: Kneels down when shown a red card
Waits patiently to be freed by a teammate
Rejoins the game once the VAR signal is complete

lks2.objective: Play a World Cup themed tag game while dribbling. Learn to accept referee decisions gracefully and use teamwork to bring players back into the game.
successCriteria: Accepts the red card without arguing
Runs to teammates to free them with the VAR signal
Keeps the ball under control while playing

uks2.objective: Combine dribbling under pressure with quick decision-making. Understand the referee's role, respect their decisions, and take responsibility as a VAR official.
successCriteria: Manages ball control while evading multiple referees
Steps up as a fair VAR official when selected
Speaks respectfully to referees even when disagreeing with a decision

space.description: Rectangular playing area sized to your group — roughly 20×15m for 15 children. Mark boundary with large cones. All children start inside with a football each.

ks1.description: Smaller area (15×12m). Keep the boundary close so it's easy to reach frozen teammates.

uks2.description: Larger area (25×18m). Gives more room for evasion and creative dribbling routes.

value.name: Respect
value.text: Football is full of decisions we disagree with — and referees are the ones making them. Respect is showing that even when you think a decision is wrong, you accept it and move on. Praise children who accept a 'red card' without complaint, and who deliver the VAR verdict fairly when it's their turn. The lesson lands loudest when parents can hear you name it.

steps: Set up a rectangular playing area with large cones. All children start inside with a football each.
Select 2–3 children to be referees. Give each one a bib and a red cone.
On your signal, referees try to tag the attackers by touching them and showing the red cone in front of them.
Once tagged, the player must go down onto their knees and 'beg' for the decision to be overturned.
To be freed, a teammate must run over to them and perform the VAR signal — drawing a square in the air with both hands.
Once the VAR check is complete, the tagged player rejoins the game with their football.
Rotate referees every 1–2 minutes so every child experiences the role.
progressions: Begin the session without footballs so children can learn the rules and rhythm of the game first.
Change the referees regularly to give different children a turn — especially quieter ones who might not volunteer.
Increase or decrease the number of referees to raise or lower the challenge for the attackers.
Progress so all children dribble a football while playing — referees included.
Select just two children as the official VAR team responsible for allowing tagged players back in — creates authority and responsibility.
Swap red cones for yellow cones — children must be tagged twice before receiving the 'red card'.
questions: How do you show respect to a referee, even when you disagree with them?
What's the difference between complaining and accepting a decision?
How does it feel when a teammate comes over quickly to free you?
As a VAR official, how do you make a fair decision under pressure?

step.space: Increase the area to create more opportunities for dribbling and escaping; reduce it to increase pressure and force quicker decisions.
step.task: Challenge children to complete a football skill, a turn or a ball mastery move before they can perform the VAR signal to free a teammate.
step.equipment: Swap red cones for yellow cones so children must be tagged twice before being sent off. Introduce gates around the area as temporary hiding spots.
step.people: Rotate the referees and VAR officials regularly to give every child a different responsibility. Increase referee count for a harder session.

base.showmanship: This is a brilliant chance to reinforce positive values around football and remind children that referees should always be treated with respect — even when we disagree with their decisions. Call it out loud when a child accepts a red card gracefully or delivers a VAR verdict fairly. Parents watching should hear the lesson land.

steps: Set up a small area with large cones. Every child starts inside with a football.
Choose 2 referees — give each a bib and a red cone.
When a referee touches a runner and shows the red cone, the runner kneels down.
A teammate runs over and draws a big square in the air with both hands to free them.
Rotate the referees every minute so everyone has a turn.
progressions: Add footballs once the rules are secure.
Encourage children to help teammates back into the game quickly.
questions: How did you feel when you were 'sent off'?
Who helped you get back into the game?

coachingCard.objective: Protect the ball, escape pressure, awareness, dribbling.
coachingCard.setup: Grid, ball each, 1–2 referees with red cones.
coachingCard.idea: I: Referees are giving red cards! D: Show tag & VAR rescue. E: Dribble, avoid tags, rescue teammates. A: Play.
coachingCard.observation: Are players recognising pressure and escaping?
coachingCard.cues: Head up · Change direction · Shield · Accelerate away.
coachingCard.interventions: ~3 mins: coaching point. ~7 mins: progression. ~11 mins: final challenge.
coachingCard.progressions: More referees · Rescue with a turn · VAR officials only · Yellow card rule.
coachingCard.differentiation: Bigger area, fewer referees, no skill condition (support). Weaker foot, turns before rescue, smaller area (stretch).
coachingCard.behaviourSafety: Safe kneeling · Fair tagging · Rescue quickly · Avoid collisions.
coachingCard.finishReflect: Finish: Can everyone avoid a red card in the final minute? Reflect: 'How did you escape pressure?' 'What helped keep the ball?'
